arc_intro:
FQ-218 — Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

FQ-142 started with an unexplained access key. Six sessions later, FoodQuick has a real architecture. Before we close this ticket — and Building Basics — I need three things from you: a dashboard that actually covers the whole stack, budget alerts that catch cost surprises early, and a portfolio narrative you could defend in an interview. Not 'I built a 3-tier app.' The WHY behind the decisions.

— Ravi
arc_outro:
Ravi Krishnan — FQ-218 closed:

Dashboard covers ALB, ASG, and RDS in one view. Budget alerts land on the same SNS channel as on-call. Docs live in S3 with a clean key structure. And your narrative connects decisions back to real FoodQuick mistakes — that's the proof, not a certificate.

FQ-142 is done. Building Basics is done. Working Level is next — on-call starts for real.

— Ravi

tasks.scenario: You open the existing foodquick-app-health CloudWatch dashboard. It only shows ALB RequestCount. ASG and RDS widgets are missing.
tasks.question: Is an ALB-only dashboard complete monitoring for FoodQuick's 3-tier architecture?
options: A) Yes — the load balancer is the only layer that matters for customer experience
B) No — a complete view needs key metrics across presentation (ALB), application (ASG), and data (RDS) tiers on one page, or you can miss app/DB failures while ALB still looks fine
C) Yes — CloudWatch only allows one metric per dashboard
D) No — you should delete the ALB widgets and only watch RDS
tasks.explanation: Dashboard's value multiple layers-ai ore in page kaatrathula is there. ALB only paathaa, app tier or RDS issue miss can happen — in C6.1 kathukkitta same principle.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — one dashboard, all three tiers. ALB alone is not the whole story.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — ALB healthy even if ASG/RDS break can happen. Full stack widgets is needed.

tasks.question: Which widget set best completes foodquick-app-health for this architecture?
options: A) Only EC2 CPU from a single instance
B) ALB RequestCount + TargetResponseTime, ASG CPUUtilization + InstanceCount, RDS CPUUtilization + DatabaseConnections
C) Only S3 BucketSizeBytes
D) Only IAM Access Analyzer findings
tasks.explanation: Presentation, application, data — moonu tier also cover aaganum. This C7.4 live build's exact widget set.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — ALB + ASG + RDS is the cohesive monitoring picture.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit incomplete. Three tiers, three metric families — ALB/ASG/RDS.

tasks.question: What is the real purpose of an AWS Budget alert in this closing lesson?
options: A) It automatically deletes expensive resources when spend rises
B) It proactively notifies the team when spend approaches or crosses a threshold — catching silent cost growth early (the C5 unmanaged growth pattern)
C) It replaces Cost Explorer entirely
D) It only works for Reserved Instances
tasks.explanation: Budget alerts automatic cost cut do not do — notify does. in C5 we saw silent S3/EFS growth like mistakes early catch to do helpful.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — notify early, don't pretend the budget deletes resources for you.
tasks.ren_wrong: Budget alert delete do not do / auto-optimize do not do — proactive notify job.

tasks.ren_correct: Correct — reuse the on-call SNS path. Cost and ops share one attention channel.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — already trusted SNS is there. That reuse do.

tasks.scenario: priya-dev prepares for an interview by memorizing the component list (ALB, ASG, RDS, S3) but not the reasoning behind security-group-per-tier or health-check path choices.
tasks.question: What is the real interview risk, and what should she prepare instead?
options: A) No risk — listing AWS services is enough for cloud roles
B) Interviewers evaluate judgment: she should practice a structured WHY narrative tying each decision to a specific FoodQuick mistake (e.g. default SG exposure), not only WHAT was built
C) She should hide that FoodQuick ever had mistakes
D) She should only talk about pricing calculators
tasks.explanation: WHAT memorized, WHY articulate to do practice or, in interview shallow theriyum. Lesson's core: portfolio = reasoned decisions.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — WHY tied to real mistakes beats a service name list.
tasks.ren_wrong: Component recall podathu. Judgment = why this design, which mistake it prevents.

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks you to pick the strongest opening line for a portfolio / interview narrative about FoodQuick.
options: A) 'I built a 3-tier architecture on AWS with ALB, ASG, and RDS.'

B) 'I redesigned FoodQuick after audit-driven failures — for example scoped security groups per tier after a default-SG path exposed the database — then verified the stack with dashboards, budgets, and a failure test, not just one successful HTTP 200.'
C) 'AWS is scalable and secure by default so design barely matters.'
D) 'I followed a YouTube tutorial exactly.'
tasks.explanation: Strong narrative = context + specific decision + verification depth. Weak narrative = service shopping list.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — specific mistake → specific design → how you verified.
tasks.ren_wrong: Shopping-list intros soft will be. Tie decisions to FoodQuick lessons.

tasks.scenario: Looking back across CS2–CS7, the same failure mode shows up in IAM offboarding, public-subnet databases, default security groups, open S3, and rushed route tables.
tasks.question: What single pattern ties those mistakes together?
options: A) AWS billing bugs
B) 'Convenience now, restrict/fix later' — temporary launch-day shortcuts that became permanent production risk
C) Only multi-region complexity
D) Only Tanglish documentation gaps
tasks.explanation: Course's recurring theme — convenience-first decisions. Recognizing one pattern across layers is mature judgment.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — one failure mode, many layers. That's the Building Basics insight.
tasks.ren_wrong: Unrelated incidents not — ore 'fix later' habit across IAM/network/storage.

tasks.scenario: Budget is created and SNS is attached, but the on-call channel never gets a test notification. Threshold is 100% of a budget set far above current spend.
tasks.error_shown: Budgets console: 'OK'. SNS topic: no recent publishes. Team: 'We never got a cost alert in staging.'
tasks.diagnosis: Alert only fires at 100% of an inflated budget, so day-to-day overruns never notify. Also no test publish was sent to confirm SNS subscription health.
tasks.fix: Add an 80% threshold (and optionally a forecasted spend alert), keep 100% as hard stop, send a test notification to foodquick-oncall-alerts, confirm subscribers confirmed the email/Slack endpoint.
tasks.explanation: Budget 'exists' != 'will warn early'. 80% + test publish = real closing check.

tasks.scenario: Meera asks whether documentation and dashboards are 'extra cost' that can be skipped now that the architecture works.
tasks.question: What's the right cost/judgment call?
tasks.solution: Observability and docs are cheap compared to the retrofit cost FoodQuick already paid across CS2–CS6. Skipping them recreates the 'works until it doesn't / can't explain why' failure mode. Budget alerts specifically exist to prevent another silent growth incident; dashboards prevent Twitter-as-monitoring. Keep both.
tasks.explanation: Working system + no proof/observability = incomplete portfolio and incomplete operations.

tasks.scenario: Time to send Ravi the FQ-218 closing report and formally end the Building Basics FoodQuick arc that started at FQ-142.

options: A) 'Everything works. Done.'

B) 'Expanded foodquick-app-health to ALB/ASG/RDS. Monthly budget with 80%/100% alerts on foodquick-oncall-alerts. Docs at portfolio/foodquick-architecture-v1/ in S3. C) 'Deleted all monitoring to save money.'
D) 'Skipped documentation because interviews don't care.'
tasks.explanation: Closing report specific must be — dashboard, budget, docs, narrative. Vague 'done' overclaim / skip docs = wrong close.
tasks.ren_correct: This correct close — evidence across monitoring, cost, docs, and interview-ready WHY.
